To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose a variant, SG-MRL, of the MAML algorithm for RL problems and prove its convergence to an \textit{epsilon}-first-order stationary point in a number of iterations that depends only on the smoothness of the objective function, the number of iterations used at test time, the accuracy parameter, and other problem-dependent constants.

we propose a new algorithm called SG-MRL for model-agnostic RL problems, and we provide a convergence guarantee for SG-MRL that is the first for such algorithms, and also show how our results can be extended to the case of multiple stochastic gradient updates.
we propose a new variant of model-agnostic meta-learning for reinforcement learning problems, and provide the first convergence guarantee of such algorithms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) Can we extend the MAML method to the RL setting? If yes, (2) how do we analyze the convergence of MAML methods for RL? and (3) what are the empirical performance of such methods?

the convergence of model-agnostic meta-learning algorithms for reinforcement learning problems, and we provide a new algorithm, Stochastic Gradient Meta-reinforcement Learning (S-GMRL), and show that it converges at a rate that matches the best-known rate for the MDP setting

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MAML is a good algorithm for meta-reinforcement-learning, and that the proposed SG-MRL is a good variant of it.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the meta-reinforcement setting where we have a large number of MDPs and each MDP is represented by a large state space, SG-MRL is more robust to hyper-parameter tuning and has better empirical performance than MAML.
we provide a theoretical analysis for the convergence of MAML methods for RL problems, and show that our proposed method is empirically competitive in several RL tasks.
we show that MAML can be applied in RL problems, where the policy gradient is approximated using stochastic gradients, and we provide a theoretical analysis that supports this application.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SG-MRL can outperform the original MAML method in terms of both performance and sample efficiency, while providing convergence guarantees.
, while MAML and SG-MRL have similar performance in practice, SG-MRL is more sample-efficient and can be used to solve problems that require multiple gradient steps at test time.
, for RL problems, stochastic gradient methods are crucial for MAML algorithms to work well in practice.
